question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-3)-\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{5} \\  & =-15-10 \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given that A=[5255−3], find the product of the eigenvalues of A.

a
25
b
−25
c
20
d
−10
e
−15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of p(λ), i.e. the eigenvalues of A, satisfy

{λ1+λ2=tr(A)λ1⋅λ2=det(A).

So, the product of the eigenvalues of A is equal to the determinant of A. Therefore, λ1⋅λ2=det(A)=|5255−3|=5⋅(−3)−5⋅25=−15−10=−25.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\sqrt{2})\cdot 2-\sqrt{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2} \\  & =-7\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Given that A=[−22232], find the product of the eigenvalues of A.

a
−42
b
−32
c
−72
d
2
e
52
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of p(λ), i.e. the eigenvalues of A, satisfy

{λ1+λ2=tr(A)λ1⋅λ2=det(A).

So, the product of the eigenvalues of A is equal to the determinant of A. Therefore, λ1⋅λ2=det(A)=|−22232|=(−22)⋅2−2⋅3=−42−32=−72.

The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\sqrt{2})\cdot 2-\sqrt{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2} \\  & =-7\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],$ find the sum of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the trace of $A.$ 

Therefore, 

$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{7}{5} & -2\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{7}{5} & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{7}{5} \\  & =-1-\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{7}{5} & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{7}{5} \\  & =-1-\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
−4
b
−52
c
32
d
72
e
−92
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of p(λ), i.e. the eigenvalues of A, satisfy

{λ1+λ2=tr(A)λ1⋅λ2=det(A).

So, the product of the eigenvalues of A is equal to the determinant of A. Therefore,

λ1⋅λ2=det(A)=|125275−2|=12⋅(−2)−52⋅75=−1−72=−92.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}-23 & -15 \\ 9 & 19\end{aligned}],$ find the sum of the eigenvalues of $A.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the trace of $A.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A)=-23+19=-4.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that A=[−23−15919], find the sum of the eigenvalues of A.

a
5
b
32
c
42
d
−2
e
−4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of p(λ), i.e. the eigenvalues of A, satisfy

{λ1+λ2=tr(A)λ1⋅λ2=det(A).

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of A is equal to the trace of A.

Therefore,

λ1+λ2=tr(A)=−23+19=−4.

question.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\text{tr}(A)=-8$ and $\text{det}(A)=12.$ Then, ${A}^{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-8A-12I.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-8A-12I.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix such that tr(A)=−8 and det(A)=12. Then, A2=

a
8A−12I
b
12A+8I
c
−8A−12I
d
−8A+12I
e
12A−8I
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by

p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA2−tr(A)A+det(A)I=OA2=tr(A)A−det(A)IA2=−8A−12I.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix such that tr(A)=3 and det(A)=−7. Then, A2=

a
3A+4I
b
3A+7I
c
3A−2I
d
A+7I
e
−8A+7I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by

p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA2−tr(A)A+det(A)I=OA2=tr(A)A−det(A)IA2=3A−(−7)IA2=3A+7I.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers

Question 8
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix such that tr(A)=−14 and det(A)=−36. Then, A2=

a
36A−14I
b
−36A+14I
c
14A−36I
d
−14A+36I
e
−14A−36I
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by

p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA2−tr(A)A+det(A)I=OA2=tr(A)A−det(A)IA2=−14A+36I.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Let $A$ be a $4\times 4$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{4}+2{\lambda }^{3}-10{\lambda }^{2}+12.$ Then, ${A}^{4}=$
question.worked_solution:
Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{4}+2{A}^{3}-10{A}^{2}+12I & =O \\ {A}^{4} & =-2{A}^{3}+10{A}^{2}-12I.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Let A be a 4×4 matrix with the characteristic polynomial p(λ)=λ4+2λ3−10λ2+12. Then, A4=

a
A3+12A2−10I
b
A3+10A2−2I
c
−2A3+10A2−12I
d
2A3−A2−12I
e
2A3−10A2+12I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA4+2A3−10A2+12I=OA4=−2A3+10A2−12I.

question.html:
Question 9
?

Let A be a 4×4 matrix with the characteristic polynomial p(λ)=λ4+2λ3−10λ2+12. Then, A4=

a
A3+12A2−10I
b
A3+10A2−2I
c
−2A3+10A2−12I
d
2A3−A2−12I
e
2A3−10A2+12I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA4+2A3−10A2+12I=OA4=−2A3+10A2−12I.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers

solution.reasoning: By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, A⁴+2A³−10A²+12I=0. Thus A⁴=−2A³+10A²−12I, which is option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\text{tr}(A)=5$ and $\text{det}(A)=9.$ Then, ${A}^{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =5A-9I.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix such that tr(A)=5 and det(A)=9. Then, A2=

a
9A−5I
b
−5A−9I
c
5A+9I
d
−9A+5I
e
5A−9I
Submit
Correct

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by

p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA2−tr(A)A+det(A)I=OA2=tr(A)A−det(A)IA2=5A−9I.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
question.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-2) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -8) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}-11\lambda +24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-2A-11I+24{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 24{A}^{-1} & =11I+2A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{11}{24}I+\frac{1}{12}A-\frac{1}{24}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

If A=[3−2−202102−3], then A−1=

a
1124I+112A−124A2
b
1112I+13A−124A2
c
24I+112A+16A2
d
1124I−16A+124A2
e
1124I+112A+112A2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's find the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0:

det(A−λI)=0|3−λ−2−202−λ102−3−λ|=0(3−λ)|2−λ12−3−λ|=0(3−λ)((2−λ)(−3−λ)−2)=0(3−λ)(λ2+λ−8)=0λ3−2λ2−11λ+24=0

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

A3−2A2−11A+24I=O.

Since A is invertible, we can multiply this equation by A−1:

A−1(A3−2A2−11A+24I)=OA2−2A−11I+24A−1=O24A−1=11I+2A−A2A−1=1124I+112A−124A2

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-2) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -8) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}-11\lambda +24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-2A-11I+24{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 24{A}^{-1} & =11I+2A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{11}{24}I+\frac{1}{12}A-\frac{1}{24}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Given that A=[3224] and A−1=pI+qA, find the value p+q.

a
74
b
58
c
14
d
34
e
98
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's find the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0: det(A−λI)=0|3−λ224−λ|=0(3−λ)(4−λ)−4=0λ2−7λ+8=0

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

A2−7A+8I=O.

Since A is invertible, we can multiply this equation by A−1:

A−1(A2−7A+8I)=OA−7I+8A−1=OA−1=78I−18A

Therefore, p=78, q=−18 and p+q=78+(−18)=34.

question.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
question.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 3 \\ 5 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((4-\lambda )^{2}-15) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-9{\lambda }^{2}+9\lambda -1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-9{A}^{2}+9A-I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-9{A}^{2}+9A-I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-9A+9I-{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =9I-9A+{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

A3−9A2+9A−I=O.

A−1(A3−9A2+9A−I)=OA2−9A+9I−A−1=OA−1=9I−9A+A2

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.
$$

Given that A=[23−45] and A−1=pI+qA, find the value of p+q.

a
−811
b
311
c
611
d
111

EXPLANATION

Let's find the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0:

det(A−λI)=0|2−λ3−45−λ|=0(2−λ)(5−λ)+12=0λ2−7λ+22=0

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

A2−7A+22I=O.

Since A is invertible, we can multiply this equation by A−1:

A−1(A2−7A+22I)=OA−7I+22A−1=OA−1=722I−122A

Therefore, p=722, q=−122, and

p+q=722+(−122)=311.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
question.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+{\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+A-7I+2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 2{A}^{-1} & =7I-A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+{\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+A-7I+2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 2{A}^{-1} & =7I-A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's find the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0:

det(A−λI)=0|2−λ110−4−λ−3011−λ|=0(2−λ)|−4−λ−311−λ|=0(2−λ)((−4−λ)(1−λ)+3)=0(2−λ)(λ2+3λ−1)=0λ3+λ2−7λ+2=0

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

A3+A2−7A+2I=O.

Since A is invertible, we can multiply this equation by A−1:

A−1(A3+A2−7A+2I)=OA2+A−7I+2A−1=O2A−1=7I−A−A2A−1=72I−12A−12A2

solution.reasoning: The characteristic polynomial is (\lambda-2)(\lambda^2+3\lambda-1)=\lambda^3+\lambda^2-7\lambda+2. Cayley–Hamilton gives A³+A²−7A+2I=0. feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+{\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+A-7I+2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 2{A}^{-1} & =7I-A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+8 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Question 16
?

Given the matrix A=[3−24−3] and f(x)=x22−x20+3x−2, find f(A).

a
[9−612−9]
b
[3112−4]
c
[4112−7]
d
[7−612−11]
e
[5−612−5]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ):

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|3−λ−24−3−λ|=(3−λ)(−3−λ)+8=λ2−1

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x20
x2−1 x22−x20+3x−2|
x22 − x20
3x − 2

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(3x−2) where q(x)=x20. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I)=q(A)⋅O+(3A−2I)=3A−2I=3[3−24−3]−2[1001]=[9−612−9]−[2002]=[7−612−11].

last_observation.name: Question 16
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+8 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{22}-{x}^{20}+3x-2\,$, find $f(A).$

Question 16
?

Given the matrix A=[3−24−3] and f(x)=x22−x20+3x−2, find f(A).

a
[9−612−9]
b
[3112−4]
c
[4112−7]
d
[7−612−11]
e
[5−612−5]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ):

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|3−λ−24−3−λ|=(3−λ)(−3−λ)+8=λ2−1

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x20
x2−1 x22−x20+3x−2|
x22 − x20
3x − 2

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(3x−2) where q(x)=x20. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I)=q(A)⋅O+(3A−2I)=3A−2I=3[3−24−3]−2[1001]=[9−612−9]−[2002]=[7−612−11].
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem

solution.reasoning: Direct multiplication gives A²=I, so A²²−A²⁰=I−I=0. Therefore f(A)=3A−2I, with rows (7,−6) and (12,−11), matching option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 16
feedback.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{22}-{x}^{20}+3x-2\,$, find $f(A).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+8 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3$, find $f(A).$
question.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}14-\lambda & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{10}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{12}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,4x$
$\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\ & =2A-3I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Question 17
?

Given the matrix A=[148−24−14] and f(x)=x12−4x10+x3−2x−3, find f(A).

a
[118−24−16]
b
[11−248−16]
c
[4024−70−44]
d
[2516−48−31]
e
[16−2518−42]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ): p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|14−λ8−24−14−λ|=(14−λ)(−14−λ)+192=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x10 + x
x2−4 x12−4x10+x3−2x−3|
x12 − 4x10
x3 − 2x − 3
x3 − 4x
2x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(2x−3) where q(x)=x10+x. Replacing x with A, we have f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore, f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(2A−3I)=2A−3I=2[148−24−14]−3[1001]=[2816−48−28]−[3003]=[2516−48−31].

last_observation.name: Question 17
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}14-\lambda & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{10}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{12}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,4x$
$\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\ & =2A-3I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 17

and $f(x)={x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3$, find $f(A).$

Given the matrix A=[148−24−14] and f(x)=x12−4x10+x3−2x−3, find f(A).

a
[118−24−16]
b
[11−248−16]
c
[4024−70−44]
d
[2516−48−31]
e
[16−2518−42]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ): p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|14−λ8−24−14−λ|=(14−λ)(−14−λ)+192=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x10 + x
x2−4 x12−4x10+x3−2x−3|
x12 − 4x10
x3 − 2x − 3
x3 − 4x
2x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(2x−3) where q(x)=x10+x. Replacing x with A, we have f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore, f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(2A−3I)=2A−3I=2[148−24−14]−3[1001]=[2816−48−28]−[3003]=[2516−48−31].

feedback.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3$, find $f(A).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}14-\lambda & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{10}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{12}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,4x$
$\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\ & =2A-3I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6$, find $f(A).$
question.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\ & =-2A+6I \\ & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

last_observation.name: Question 18
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\ & =-2A+6I \\ & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6$, find $f(A).$

$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$

Question 18
?

Given the matrix A=[611−3−6] and f(x)=x15−3x13+x3−5x+6, find f(A).

a
[−22−6618]
b
[−12−22612]
c
[−6−22618]
d
[−6−22186]
e
[18−226−6]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ): p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|6−λ11−3−6−λ|=(6−λ)(−6−λ)+33=λ2−3

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x13 + x
x2−3 x15−3x13+x3−5x+6|
x15 − 3x13
x3 − 5x + 6
x3 − 3x
− 2x + 6

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(−2x+6) where q(x)=x13+x. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(−2A+6I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(−2A+6I)=q(A)⋅O+(−2A+6I)=−2A+6I=−2[611−3−6]+6[1001]=[−12−22612]+[6006]=[−6−22618].
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem

solution.reasoning: Direct multiplication gives A²=3I. Thus A¹⁵−3A¹³=A¹³(A²−3I)=0 and A³=3A. Therefore f(A)=−2A+6I, with rows (−6,−22) and (6,18), matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 18
feedback.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6$, find $f(A).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\ & =-2A+6I \\ & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$
question.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Question 19
?

Given the matrix A=[42−6−4] and f(x)=x16−4x14+7x−3, find f(A).

a
[2512−24−31]
b
[311442−25]
c
[2514−42−31]
d
[1514−4230]
e
[25−4214−31]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ):

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|4−λ2−6−4−λ|=(4−λ)(−4−λ)+12=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x14
x2−4 x16−4x14+7x−3|
x16 − 4x14
7x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(7x−3) where q(x)=x14. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(7A−3I)=7A−3I=7[42−6−4]−3[1001]=[2814−42−28]−[3003]=[2514−42−31].
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem

solution.reasoning: Direct multiplication gives A²=4I, so A¹⁶−4A¹⁴=A¹⁴(A²−4I)=0. Therefore f(A)=7A−3I, with rows (25,14) and (−42,−31), matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Given the matrix A=[42−6−4] and f(x)=x16−4x14+7x−3, find f(A).

a
[2512−24−31]
b
[311442−25]
c
[2514−42−31]
d
[1514−4230]

[25−4214−31]
Submit

EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ):

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|4−λ2−6−4−λ|=(4−λ)(−4−λ)+12=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x14
x2−4 x16−4x14+7x−3|
x16 − 4x14
7x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(7x−3) where q(x)=x14. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(7A−3I)=7A−3I=7[42−6−4]−3[1001]=[2814−42−28]−[3003]=[2514−42−31].

question.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ then ${A}^{3}=$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ using long division:
$\,\,x$ $+$ $1$
${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\phantom{|}\,\,}$
${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $-$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $+$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $-$ $20$
$21x$ $+$ $20$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)=x+1.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\ & =21A+20I.\end{aligned} $$

21A+20I

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's divide the polynomial f(x)=x3 by characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2−x−20, using long division:

x + 1
x2−x−20 x3|
x3 − x2 − 20x
x2 + 20x
x2 − x − 20
21x + 20

Therefore, we can write x3 as

x3=q(x)p(x)+(21x+20), where q(x)=x+1. Replacing x with A, we have

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I).

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I)=q(A)⋅O+(21A+20I)=21A+20I.

Question 20
?

If A is a 2×2 matrix A with characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2−x−20, then A3=

a
−21A+20I
b
20A+21I
c
−20A−21I
d
21A−20I
e
21A+20I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's divide the polynomial f(x)=x3 by characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2−x−20, using long division:

x + 1
x2−x−20 x3|
x3 − x2 − 20x
x2 + 20x
x2 − x − 20
21x + 20

Therefore, we can write x3 as

x3=q(x)p(x)+(21x+20), where q(x)=x+1. Replacing x with A, we have

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I).

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I)=q(A)⋅O+(21A+20I)=21A+20I.

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),
$$

 which we call the **characteristic polynomial** of the matrix $A.$

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/e023f473557611b3b3dd0234e4135bc910ea1f22acf197171b0169c08e62c7b6.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),

tutorial.problem:
What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/a76f0ebcede66bcb468bb7554fd622e96d91dc55450acf88678be83883e04b5f.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

steps.name: Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda),$ i.e., the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the trace of $A.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\lambda_1+\lambda_2 = \textrm{tr}(A)= 9+(-6)=3.
$$

steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-3)-\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{5} \\  & =-15-10 \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\sqrt{2})\cdot 2-\sqrt{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2} \\  & =-7\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

tutorial.name: The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
tutorial.problem:
The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/8d009abd836832657b7350553fbf3c34ed8667f0eda65c59742fb071ea54bfb6.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/8d009abd836832657b7350553fbf3c34ed8667f0eda65c59742fb071ea54bfb6.svg)

steps.name: Example: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-4A+18I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y = -4+18 = 14.$

question.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\textrm{tr}(A)=-4$ and $\textrm{det}(A)=-18.$ If $A^2 = xA + yI$ for constants $x$ and $y,$ then find the value of $x+y.$
question.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\textrm{tr}(A)\lambda+\textrm{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-4A+18I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y = -4+18 = 14.$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let A be a 2×2 matrix such that tr(A)=3 and det(A)=−7. Then, A2=

a
3A+4I
b
3A+7I
c
3A−2I
d
A+7I
e
−8A+7I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The characteristic polynomial of A is given by

p(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A).

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

p(A)=OA2−tr(A)A+det(A)I=OA2=tr(A)A−det(A)IA2=3A−(−7)IA2=3A+7I.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers

steps.name: Question 8
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers
steps.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-14A+36I.\end{aligned}
$$

steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers
steps.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\textrm{det}(A-\lambda I)=0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+54 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}+A-2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}+A-2I) & =O \\ A+I-2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}I\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\dfrac{1}{2},$ $q=\dfrac{1}{2},$ and 

$$
p+q=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=1.
$$

$$

det(A−λI)=0|3−λ−2−202−λ102−3−λ|=0(3−λ)|2−λ12−3−λ|=0(3−λ)((2−λ)(−3−λ)−2)=0(3−λ)(λ2+λ−8)=0λ3−2λ2−11λ+24=0

A3−2A2−11A+24I=O.

steps.name: Question 12
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
steps.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.

tutorial.name: Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial
tutorial.problem:
If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/3eadfd94d1cd67381127bf8df9e212ab73b7cad1b2d69d05a46cebb93a102683.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/077f272847b4727ff2ddbbbff9c2b513b4ab9c55d67962189a0bbeef5fa4335d.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this.

tutorial.content:
If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/3eadfd94d1cd67381127bf8df9e212ab73b7cad1b2d69d05a46cebb93a102683.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228497/assets/077f272847b4727ff2ddbbbff9c2b513b4ab9c55d67962189a0bbeef5fa4335d.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this.

steps.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & -5 \\ 3 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+15 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\:\:x^{10}$
$x^2-1\:$ $\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{x^{12} \, - \, x^{10} + 2x - 1 {\phantom{|}} }$
$x^{12}$ $-$ $x^{10}$
$2x$ $-$ $1$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & ={x}^{10}({x}^{2}-1)+(2x-1),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x) = x^{10}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A) = q(A)p(A)+(2A-I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-I) \\ & =2A-I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -10 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+8 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|3−λ−24−3−λ|=(3−λ)(−3−λ)+8=λ2−1

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A−2I)=q(A)⋅O+(3A−2I)=3A−2I=3[3−24−3]−2[1001]=[9−612−9]−[2002]=[7−612−11].

steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
steps.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}14-\lambda & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{10}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{12}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,4x$
$\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\ & =2A-3I \\ & =2[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Given the matrix A=[148−24−14] and f(x)=x12−4x10+x3−2x−3, find f(A).

EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ): p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|14−λ8−24−14−λ|=(14−λ)(−14−λ)+192=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x10 + x
x2−4 x12−4x10+x3−2x−3|
x12 − 4x10
x3 − 2x − 3
x3 − 4x
2x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(2x−3) where q(x)=x10+x. Replacing x with A, we have f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore, f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(2A−3I)=2A−3I=2[148−24−14]−3[1001]=[2816−48−28]−[3003]=[2516−48−31].

steps.name: Question 18
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
steps.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\ & =-2A+6I \\ & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
Given the matrix
$\,A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]$
and $f(x)={x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6$, find $f(A).$
question.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$: $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{13}$ $+$ $x$
${x}^{2}-3\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{15}$ $\,\,\,\,-$ $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,5x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ $-\,\,$ $\,\,3x$
$-\,\,$ $\,\,2x$ $\,\,\,\,\,+$ $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\ & =-2A+6I \\ & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Question 18

Given the matrix A=[611−3−6] and f(x)=x15−3x13+x3−5x+6, find f(A).

a
[−22−6618]
b
[−12−22612]
c
[−6−22618]
d
[−6−22186]
e
[18−226−6]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ): p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|6−λ11−3−6−λ|=(6−λ)(−6−λ)+33=λ2−3

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x13 + x
x2−3 x15−3x13+x3−5x+6|
x15 − 3x13
x3 − 5x + 6
x3 − 3x
− 2x + 6

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(−2x+6) where q(x)=x13+x. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(−2A+6I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(−2A+6I)=q(A)⋅O+(−2A+6I)=−2A+6I=−2[611−3−6]+6[1001]=[−12−22612]+[6006]=[−6−22618].

steps.name: Question 19
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
steps.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

question.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$

$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Question 19
?

Given the matrix A=[42−6−4] and f(x)=x16−4x14+7x−3, find f(A).

a
[2512−24−31]
b
[311442−25]
c
[2514−42−31]
d
[1514−4230]
e
[25−4214−31]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial p(λ):

p(λ)=det(A−λI)=|4−λ2−6−4−λ|=(4−λ)(−4−λ)+12=λ2−4

Now, let's divide f(x) by p(x) using long division:

x14
x2−4 x16−4x14+7x−3|
x16 − 4x14
7x − 3

Therefore, we can write f(x) as f(x)=q(x)p(x)+r(x)=q(x)p(x)+(7x−3) where q(x)=x14. Replacing x with A, we have

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I).

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A−3I)=q(A)⋅O+(7A−3I)=7A−3I=7[42−6−4]−3[1001]=[2814−42−28]−[3003]=[2514−42−31].

steps.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ using long division:
$\,\,x$ $+$ $1$
${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\phantom{|}\,\,}$
${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $-$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $+$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $-$ $20$
$21x$ $+$ $20$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)=x+1.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\ & =21A+20I.\end{aligned} $$

Question 20
?

If A is a 2×2 matrix A with characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2−x−20, then A3=

a
−21A+20I
b
20A+21I
c
−20A−21I
d
21A−20I
e
21A+20I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's divide the polynomial f(x)=x3 by characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2−x−20, using long division:

x + 1
x2−x−20 x3|
x3 − x2 − 20x
x2 + 20x
x2 − x − 20
21x + 20

Therefore, we can write x3 as

x3=q(x)p(x)+(21x+20), where q(x)=x+1. Replacing x with A, we have

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I).

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

A3=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I)=q(A)⋅O+(21A+20I)=21A+20I.

questions.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-3)-\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{5} \\  & =-15-10 \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],$ then ${A}^{-1}=$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-2) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -8) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}-11\lambda +24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-2A-11I+24{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 24{A}^{-1} & =11I+2A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{11}{24}I+\frac{1}{12}A-\frac{1}{24}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{22}-{x}^{20}+3x-2\,$, find $f(A).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda & -2 \\ 4 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+8 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-1\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$
$3x$ $-$ $2$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$
